newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rivalry in Africa belongs to past - Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Rivalry in Africa belongs to past - Chirac.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, in a thinly-veiled reference to jostling with Washington, said on Wednesday rivalry between outside powers for influence in Africa should be a thing of the past.
"The time is no longer right for rivalries which harken back to another age," Chirac told Paris-based foreign diplomats at a New Year's greetings ceremony.

"Europeans and Americans must together bring their full support to African states," Chirac said. "Our countries must mobilise to bring aid to hundreds of thousands of (African) men, women and children who are abandoned."

Chirac said he regretted that a French-proposed international force to aid displaced Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire never got off the ground. He repeated a long-held French proposal for the holding of a regional peace conference.
The United States agreed to join the Zaire force after weeks of bickering between the two allies.

They clashed again just before the November U.S. presidential election when French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain said it was only when black American voters were about to go to the polls that Washington showed an interest in Africa.

He was commenting on what he said was the first visit to the continent of U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher who had been in office for nearly four years during which he visited the Middle East about 40 times. Washington angrily complained at the charge.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette played down Franco-U.S. differences on issues ranging from NATO to the United Nations on Tuesday, saying he hoped for "the greatest friendship, the fewest clashes" with Washington in 1997.

France and the United States are currently at odds over French demands that a European take charge of NATO's southern command from an American officer under reforms of the alliance after the Cold War.
The two nations also clashed in recent weeks on the appointment of Ghana's Kofi Annan as U.N. Secretary-General and differed on policies for Iraq and Zaire.

Chirac said on Wednesday that Annan "could count on the support of France." He also said the United States, Europe and Middle East countries should join together to bring a current impasse in progress towards Mideast peace because such a freeze would lead to "violence, terrorism and destablisation."
